opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, there wasn't one single reason. It was more a combination of things that came together at the right moment.

The first thing is the people. When I talked with the team, I felt there was a very strong group of researchers who really care about pushing the frontier, not just shipping a product. That kind of environment matters a lot to me. You learn the most when the people around you are better than you at many things.

The second is resources and scale. A lot of the questions I find most interesting right now only really show up when you train at large scale and see how a model actually behaves as a whole system. Google has the compute, the infrastructure, and the long history of research to make that possible. For someone who wants to understand how these models work, not just write papers about small settings, that's very attractive.

The third is more personal. My background is not originally in AI, and I've always been drawn to problems where there's still a lot of fundamental understanding missing. Large models are like that right now. We can build them and they work surprisingly well, but our understanding of why, and of how to make them reliably better at things like reasoning, is still very incomplete. Being somewhere I can work on that directly, with real models, felt like the right place to be.

And finally, a bit of timing. This field moves so fast that the next couple of years probably matter a lot. I wanted to be close to where the important work is happening, and Gemini felt like one of those places.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the simplest answer is that I wanted to be where the frontier was moving fastest, and where I could actually touch the thing I'd spent years thinking about from the outside.

For a long time my work was about agents — ReAct, Tree of Thoughts, SWE-bench, that whole line of trying to get language models to think and act in the world. And the uncomfortable truth I kept running into was that the bottleneck wasn't the agent scaffolding anymore. It was the model itself. You can design the most elegant reasoning framework you want, but once the base model gets good enough, a lot of that scaffolding just dissolves into the model's own capabilities. So at some point I had to ask myself: do I want to keep building clever wrappers around someone else's model, or do I want to go work on the model?

Gemini was attractive for a few concrete reasons. One is scale — Google has the compute, the infrastructure, the data pipelines, and a long history of doing the unglamorous engineering well. Two is that the team there genuinely cared about reasoning and agents as a first-class research direction, not as an afterthought bolted on after pretraining. When I talked to people, the conversations were about things like how to train models to explore, how to get reinforcement learning to work on long-horizon tasks, how to build evaluations that actually mean something — the exact questions I'd been obsessing over.

And the third reason is more personal. I think we're entering what I've called the second half of AI, where the hard part isn't inventing new methods but figuring out what problems to solve and how to measure real utility. That's a question you can only answer well if you're close to a frontier system and the people deploying it. Gemini gave me that proximity.

So it wasn't really a hard decision. It felt like the natural next step for the questions I was already asking.

astra-6.text: For me, the appeal is the opportunity to bring research and building useful systems closer together. I’m particularly interested in how models can go beyond answering questions—how they can use tools, interact with an environment, and carry out tasks. Working on Gemini is a chance to explore those questions in the context of a general-purpose model, where improving the underlying capabilities and learning from real applications can inform each other.

A lot of my research has been about how to move beyond answering a question to actually solving a problem—taking actions, getting feedback, and learning from that process. Gemini felt like a place where I could pursue those questions while working closely with the people building the underlying models.
